newsitem.title: USA: Albright to attend handover of Hong Kong to China.
newsitem.headline: Albright to attend handover of Hong Kong to China.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Tuesday announced plans to visit Hong Kong when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
In a speech to the U.S. Naval Academy, she also said Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen would come to Washington later this month. She gave no date.

By accepting an invitation from Britain and China to represent the United States at the handover ceremonies, "I will underline American support for the continuation of Hong Kong's current way of life and freedoms," Albright said.
"And I will emphasize America's continued involvement in protecting our interests and supporting Hong Kong's people as they enter the Chinese nation," she said.

Albright met Hong Kong democracy activist Martin Lee on Monday at the State Department in Washington and he urged her to visit the colony for the handover. State Department officials said Lee's views had convinced her to go.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright had not yet decided whether to make any other stops on her way to or from Hong Kong.
Albright said she told Lee, a Hong Kong legislator and head of the colony's Democratic Party, "the United States is deeply committed to freedom and democracy in Hong Kong."
She noted 40,000 Americans live in Hong Kong, Americans have $13 billion in investments there and "we have an interest in law enforcement and port access for Navy ships."
"Advancing these interests depends on the rule of law and protection of civil liberties in Hong Kong," she said.

The White House was criticized when Vice President Al Gore bypassed Hong Kong on a trip to Asia last month that included a controversial stop in Beijing. Gore was faulted for not stressing China's poor human rights record as forcefully as House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who also was in Beijing.
Albright also skipped Hong Kong when she visited Beijing on her February tour of major European and Asian capitals.
Nevertheless, senior U.S. officials have repeatedly stressed that China's treatment of Hong Kong will be a major factor in the development of Sino-American ties.

Albright said Chinese people possess "far more options in their daily lives than did their parents" and there has been progress in revising civil and criminal law and in permitting "a degree of choice" in village elections.

But Beijing's repression of political dissent has not changed and Washington "will continue to shine a spotlight on egregious violations of internationally-recognized human rights in China," she said.

"The world cannot and should not be allowed to forget such dissidents as Wei Jingsheng and Wang Dan, both of whom have been sentenced to long prison terms in jail for their non-violent support of democracy," she said.
The United States co-sponsored with Denmark in the U.N. Human Rights Commission a resolution faulting China's rights record but Beijing prevailed Tuesday in blocking action.
"We regret that decision," Albright said.
Despite major rows over rights, Albright cited U.S.-China cooperation on other fronts, and said the trend would be toward greater interaction.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin are to hold a summit later this year.

Albright on Tuesday reiterated the U.S. view that linking Most Favored Nation trading benefits to China's rights record would be unproductive. U.S. lawmakers increasingly have questioned whether MFN should be renewed for China.
In her speech, which ranged broadly over Asian issues, Albright also slammed Burma's military government for failing to respond to U.S. appeals to improve human rights.

"Burmese leaders are on notice that, unless the clouds of repression are lifted, they will face investment sanctions under U.S. law," she said. Clinton has the power to impose sanctions when he deems necessary.

Burns called Albright's remarks a stiffening of the U.S. position. "It puts squarely before the Burmese dictators the proposition that without an improvement in the human rights situation there is going to be action by the United States," he said.
